title: Repairing the world
hook: Jews across communities speak of repairing the world through justice and service

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jewish music, from Miriam's timbrel to the wordless niggun, and the line the music. Did you send one song to someone? Today, two Hebrew words with a long road behind them. Day one thousand fifty-three.

Two Hebrew words turn up on banners at food drives. On youth group T-shirts. In sermons about hunger, refugees, the climate. Tikkun olam. Repairing the world. Some people hear them as a modern slogan, something a committee came up with. But these words are old, and the road they took to reach a T-shirt runs through a law court, a prayer said at the end of services, and a mystical teaching about scattered light. Today's word is tikkun olam, and it has more layers than the banner shows.
screen: `BANNERS, T-SHIRTS, SERMONS.` → `TIKKUN OLAM.` → `OLDER THAN THE BANNER.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repairing, or setting right. Olam means world. The phrase appears in the Mishnah, in a chapter about divorce law, and it's surprisingly practical. A husband who had sent his wife a divorce document could once cancel it before a court in another town, without her knowing. She might remarry, believing she was free, when she wasn't. Rabban Gamliel the Elder put a stop to that, and the Mishnah gives the reason: for the repair of the world. The same reason is given for other rulings that close loopholes and protect people who could be harmed. So the first layer is legal. Repairing the world means fixing the rules so the vulnerable aren't left exposed. The second layer is prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of services, looks toward a day when the world will be set right under the sovereignty of God. Repair, there, is a hope as wide as the whole earth. The third layer comes from the mystics of Safed. In a teaching that tradition links to Rabbi Isaac Luria, divine light was scattered into the world in sparks, and each good deed and each commandment lifts a spark back up. Every small act becomes part of mending something cosmic. And then the modern layer: justice and service. The Torah's line sits underneath it: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." Jewish communities lean on these layers differently. Some put social justice at the center. Others say the commandments themselves, prayer, Shabbat, study, are how the world is repaired. Some hold both. And the Mishnah adds a line from Rabbi Tarfon, here in paraphrase: it isn't on you to finish the work, and you aren't free to walk away from it. Today's line: repair the world.
screen: `A LOOPHOLE CLOSED IN A COURT.` · `A PRAYER FOR A WORLD SET RIGHT.` · `SCATTERED SPARKS LIFTED UP.` · `JUSTICE, JUSTICE SHALT THOU FOLLOW.` · then, large: `REPAIR THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: volunteer for one hour. The hour comes later. This sit is for choosing it. Breathe slowly, and let one thing in your neighborhood that's broken come to mind. A lonely neighbor. A food bank that's short-handed. A park full of litter. A child who needs help reading. Don't try to fix the whole world. Rabbi Tarfon already let you off that. Just choose one hour and one place. Picture yourself walking in the door. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for strength for that hour. If you don't, simply hold the picture and decide. The bell holds the time.
Tikkun olam. Repairing the world: a court's reason for protecting the vulnerable, a prayer's hope, scattered sparks, and justice and service today. Today's word.
Your line: repair the world. Today, put that one hour on your calendar, with a time and a place, so it isn't just a hope. Day one thousand fifty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish communities speak of tikkun olam in volunteering, giving and social justice work, in the Aleinu prayer said at the end of services, and in the teaching that the commandments themselves help set the world right; communities weigh these differently.

fork.setup: you're a judge. a husband can cancel a divorce in a court in another town, without his wife knowing. she may remarry believing she's free. what do you rule?
options: leave the law as it is; the procedure is valid.
stop the secret cancellation, for the repair of the world.
let each town's court decide for itself.
fork.reveal: Rabban Gamliel the Elder stopped it, and the Mishnah gives the reason: for the repair of the world. the phrase begins as a way to protect someone who could be harmed.

what it means: repairing the world through justice, service, prayer and the commandments, weighted differently by different communities.
what a scholar hears: a Mishnah legal reason for protective rulings, the Aleinu's hope, and the Safed teaching of sparks lifted up.
